opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few reasons.

The first is simply economics. Scaling works, and the scaling laws are real, but they're power laws. Each additional bit of improvement costs you a multiplicative increase in compute, data, and energy. At some point the curve gets so flat that pushing further is only feasible for a handful of players, and even for them the marginal return on the next tenfold investment becomes hard to justify. When everyone is riding the same curve with roughly the same recipe, the differentiation goes away. You end up competing on who can raise the most money and build the biggest data center, and that's not a sustainable kind of advantage.

The second reason is data. High-quality human-generated text is finite, and we're already close to consuming most of what's publicly available. You can generate synthetic data, but then the question becomes how you make sure the model is actually learning something new rather than just reinforcing its own distribution. That's not a scaling question. It's a question about learning algorithms, about how you do exploration, how you verify, and how the model improves itself in a meaningful way.

The third reason, and the one I personally care most about, is that we still don't really understand why these models work. We train them with gradient descent on huge amounts of data, and representations emerge, reasoning emerges, but the mechanism is largely a black box. In my own research I've tried to look at the training dynamics. How does attention pick up structure? How do features form? Why do certain representations show up? Every time you get even a little insight there, you find the current approach is quite wasteful. A lot of compute is spent learning things that, if you understood the structure, you could learn much more efficiently. So I believe the next big leap will come from understanding: better architectures, better optimization, better ways to use memory, and better ways for models to do search and planning at inference time, instead of just making the same thing bigger.

If you look at history, that's usually how it goes. Brute force gets you surprisingly far, and then it hits a wall, and the people who understood the underlying principles are the ones who find the next path. AlphaGo is a good example. It wasn't just a bigger network. It combined learning with search in a clever way, and that's what made the difference.

So my view is that scaling is necessary but not sufficient. In the long run, the teams that win on frontier capability will be the ones that find new ideas making each unit of compute and each unit of data count for much more. That kind of innovation can come from small teams too, which is exciting, because it means the game isn't only about who has the most GPUs.

r001.rationale: It says each additional bit of improvement requires a multiplicative increase in compute, data, and energy.

r002.rationale: It says further scaling will become difficult to justify and that future gains will require new, more efficient ideas.

r003.rationale: It does not mention NeoLabs or attribute investment in it to an anticipated need for alternatives to scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that scaling has worked remarkably well, and that's exactly why it can't be the whole story going forward.

When everyone has access to the same recipe, more data, more compute, bigger transformers, the differences between labs shrink. You see this already: the top models from different companies converge on very similar benchmark numbers within months of each other. Scaling is a known path, and a known path is not a durable advantage. It becomes a capital question rather than a research question, and capital eventually gets matched.

The second issue is that the inputs are running out, or at least getting expensive in ways that don't scale cleanly. High-quality human text is finite. We've essentially consumed the internet. Synthetic data helps, but you can't bootstrap indefinitely from a model's own outputs without careful design, or you end up amplifying its blind spots. Compute keeps growing, but the energy and hardware costs grow with it, and the returns per dollar flatten. Loss curves keep improving on a log scale, but the capabilities people actually care about, reliable reasoning, planning over long horizons, knowing what you don't know, don't improve at the same rate.

And that's the third point, which I find most interesting as a researcher. There are capabilities that scaling just doesn't buy you efficiently. A model trained to predict the next token learns a lot of pattern-matching, but things like searching through a space of possibilities, verifying its own answers, or forming an abstraction and reusing it across problems are not naturally what that objective optimizes. You can approximate them with enough scale, but it's wasteful. A small amount of the right structure, whether that's search, better training objectives, or architectures that handle memory and reasoning more explicitly, can be worth orders of magnitude of raw parameters.

So my view is that the next phase of competition is about algorithmic efficiency and new ideas: how do you get more capability per unit of data and compute, and how do you get capabilities that don't emerge from pretraining alone. The labs that win won't just be the ones with the biggest clusters. They'll be the ones who figure out what to do with them that nobody else has figured out yet.

r001.rationale: The response says compute, energy, and hardware costs are growing and returns per dollar are flattening, but it does not state that capability gains from scaling require exponentially increasing resources.

r002.rationale: It anticipates competition shifting toward algorithmic efficiency and new ideas, but does not clearly say that scaling will become unaffordable and that this will drive the search for alternatives.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention NeoLabs or explain investment in it.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling is still very powerful. If you put in more compute, more data, and more engineering effort, you can still improve the model. But that doesn’t mean this is an unlimited path, or that it’s enough to maintain an advantage.

The key question is the marginal return: how much additional capability do you get for each additional dollar? If the next improvement requires dramatically more compute, then fewer companies can afford to pursue it. And if those companies are all using similar recipes, their capabilities may converge. You need some way to get more intelligence out of the same resources.

Reasoning is a good example. A model can spend more time generating an answer, but more tokens don’t automatically mean better thinking. It needs to explore useful possibilities, recognize mistakes, and verify whether it has actually solved the problem. That creates room for innovation in training, search, and how the model receives feedback.

So I wouldn’t say innovation replaces scaling. Innovation makes scaling more effective. A better algorithm can change what you get from a fixed compute budget, and then you can scale that algorithm. The frontier will depend on both.

r001.rationale: The response says the next improvement may require “dramatically more compute,” but does not state that resources must increase exponentially.

r002.rationale: It explains that rising compute costs could put further scaling beyond many companies’ reach, creating a need to get more intelligence from the same resources through innovation.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention NeoLabs or connect willingness to invest in it with the anticipated need for alternatives to scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling will continue to help. But if everyone is using similar architectures, similar data, and similar training recipes, then the competition becomes largely about who can afford more compute. You can get ahead that way, but it’s difficult to maintain a lasting advantage, because other companies can follow the same recipe.

The deeper question is whether we’re using that compute efficiently. For example, generating a longer chain of reasoning doesn’t necessarily mean the model is making progress. It might repeat itself or pursue a wrong direction. Can it recognize that, backtrack, and try a better approach? Can it learn something useful from a failed attempt? Those are questions about how the system reasons and learns, not simply how large it is.

So I don’t see scaling and innovation as opposing approaches. Scaling gives us a stronger foundation, and innovation changes what we can do with that foundation. To keep pushing the frontier, eventually you need both.

r001.rationale: The response says competing with similar approaches depends on who can afford more compute, but it does not state that scaling alone requires exponentially increasing resources.

r002.rationale: It argues that lasting progress requires both scaling and innovation, but does not predict scaling will become unaffordable or that this will drive the search for alternatives.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention NeoLabs or explain why anyone is willing to invest in it.
